**A2UI** — The only candidate where the agent-facing artifact and the human-facing artifact are the same thing: an agent describes an interactive UI as a stream of JSON messages that a client app renders with its own native widgets ([How A2UI Works](https://a2ui.org/concepts/overview/)). A catalog is a contract between agent and renderer, so the agent only sends component types and properties the renderer can build natively, never raw HTML, CSS or executable scripts; renderers advertise `supportedCatalogIds` and the agent sets a `catalogId` per surface ([Catalogs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/catalogs/)). Native coverage decided it: shipped renderer SDKs for Flutter (`a2ui_flutter`), React, Lit, Angular, SwiftUI (`A2UISwiftUI`) and Jetpack Compose (`androidx.a2ui.compose` plus `material3-a2ui`), with Core SDKs in TypeScript, Python, Dart, Swift and Kotlin ([SDKs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/)). Security is architectural: functions are catalog-defined abstractions that avoid sending raw executable code across the wire, and the spec requires that execution-boundary verification (`allowedCallers`) and user-activation checks (`requiresUserActivation`) be enforced at runtime by the renderer, while `@accessibility` must map onto WAI-ARIA, Flutter Semantics and Android/iOS accessibility APIs and Decoupled Branding lets host theming apply ([v1.0 spec](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/)). Trade-off: it is a protocol, not a visual language, so I still own tokens and styling, and the roadmap admits that today a custom component still needs an implementation on each native platform, with described primitives, a runtime templating engine and a component sandbox still ahead ([roadmap](https://a2ui.org/roadmap/)).

actions.evaluations:
**A2UI** — The agent-facing artifact and the human-facing artifact are the same thing: an agent describes an interactive UI as a stream of JSON messages that a client app renders with its own native widgets ([Overview](https://a2ui.org/concepts/overview/)). A catalog is a contract between agent and renderer, so the agent only sends component types and properties the renderer can build natively, never raw HTML, CSS or executable scripts; renderers advertise `supportedCatalogIds` and the agent sets a `catalogId` per surface ([Catalogs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/catalogs/)). Native coverage decided it: the project says "the same agent streams UI to multiple platforms or frameworks, such as Flutter, React, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose" and "WebViews or HTML are not required," with published packages for Python, TypeScript, Dart/Flutter (`a2ui_core`, `a2ui_agent`, `a2ui_flutter`) and Swift (`A2UISwiftCore`, `A2UISwiftUI`), plus the AndroidX Compose renderer ([README](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui), [SDKs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/)). It also treats the design system as the contract: catalogs hold components, functions, prompt instructions and design tokens, and the spec notes "most production applications will define their own catalog to reflect their specific design system." Functions are "catalog-defined abstractions that avoid sending raw executable code across the wire," with `allowedCallers` and `requiresUserActivation` enforced at runtime by the renderer, and the Catalog-Agnostic Accessibility Requirements bind `@accessibility` to WAI-ARIA, Flutter Semantics and Android/iOS accessibility APIs ([v1.0 spec](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/)). Trade-off: it is a protocol, not a visual language, so I still own tokens and styling, and the roadmap admits a custom component still needs an implementation on each native platform today ([roadmap](https://a2ui.org/roadmap/)).

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Strong Android design system with color roles, typography, shapes and dynamic color ([Material 3](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)), but Kotlin-only and a widget API rather than a wire format. Google's own agentic path treats Material 3 as a catalog implementation: the Compose A2UI renderer is "design-system agnostic" and ships a "Built-in Basic Catalog (`androidx.compose.material3:material3-a2ui`)" where the catalog "acts as a contract that defines the specific UI elements, properties, and functions available to the agent" ([Compose A2UI renderer](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/agentic)). M3 is the Android visual layer inside an A2UI catalog.

**AI Elements** — Its README says it moves to shadcn/ui and will be deprecated at the end of November 2026; the Reasoning, Tool and Plan patterns now live in shadcn on a shared `Trace` shape ([repo](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements), [docs](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements)). Copy-in React/Tailwind, no native path, published end date.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — Deepest native Apple ergonomics, but the HIG is prose guidance, not a machine-readable contract, and SwiftUI is Apple-only with no agent-facing surface concept ([SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)). I would pair it with A2UI's `A2UISwiftUI` renderer.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — Tokens for colors, typography, spacing, shadows and surfaces, Tailwind 4, Radix-based components, React 18/19 required; but the provider and `TextLink`/`ButtonLink` router handling only make sense inside ChatGPT ([README](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)). A dead end for anything that must also ship natively.

**Fluent UI** — React v9, legacy v8 and Web Components with Griffel styling and a documented migration path ([README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui)), but all DOM-targeted and Copilot-shaped rather than protocol-shaped. A Fluent-flavored A2UI catalog would change my mind.

**json-render** — Closest rival: `defineCatalog`, `defineRegistry`, `Renderer` and `catalog.prompt()` with packages for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, shadcn/ui, React Native, Next.js, Remotion, React PDF, React Email, Chat SDK, Ink, Satori, MCP Apps and YAML, advertising cross-platform as "React, Vue, Svelte, Solid (web), React Native (mobile) from the same catalog" ([README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render)). I still pick A2UI because its clients stop at React Native: no SwiftUI, Compose or Flutter renderer.

**Radix UI** — The best unstyled accessibility layer on the web, but its MCP server helps coding agents compose primitives rather than making UI an agent surface; no native renderer, no shared wire format ([README](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives)).

**Vercel UI SDK** — A behaviors library (focus, selection, dismissal, popups, drag and drop) in `@ui-sdk/core` with adapters for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components, plus `agent.snapshot()`, `agent.act()`, `agent.query()` and an installable skill; but "UI SDK is currently in beta and subject to the Vercel beta terms" and there is no native target ([docs](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent), [README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui)).

**shadcn/ui** — Now hosts the agentic patterns AI Elements used to carry, on a shared `Trace` shape ([AI Elements](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements)); my pick for the web visual layer on top of A2UI, though alone it is web-only and offers patterns rather than a renderable contract.

**CopilotKit** — The most complete product stack here: chat, generative UI, shared state, human-in-the-loop and frontend tools over AG-UI, with "CopilotKit now speaks AG-UI 1.0 and the A2UI 1.0 spec for declarative generative UI" and generative UI ranging "from your own components to A2UI specs to sandboxed MCP Apps" ([README](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit), [docs](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/concepts/generative-ui-overview)). I still prefer A2UI because CopilotKit delegates declarative generative UI to the A2UI spec while keeping the runtime React-first, with native reach via React Native rather than SwiftUI or Compose.

**MCP Apps** — The standard for interactive tool UIs in chat hosts: a tool declares a `ui://` resource containing its HTML interface, "the host fetches the resource and displays it in a sandboxed iframe," with bidirectional calls, unchanged wire protocol between 1.x and 2.x, and hosts including Claude, ChatGPT and VS Code ([README](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps)). The payload is HTML rather than native widgets, so it is delivery, not composition.

**Tamagui** — An optimizing compiler that flattens styled components to a div plus atomic CSS on web or a View with hoisted style objects on native ([README](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui)); native means React Native, and there is no agent-facing surface.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — The most rigorous accessibility work in the field, with `@react-aria/mcp` and an Agent Skill, but React-only with no native renderer and no agent-renderable surface format ([README](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)).

**Chakra UI** — Accessible React components with a first-party MCP server ([README](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)); a fine web component layer, but web-only and with no agent-authored surface format.

**Flutter** — One codebase for mobile, web and desktop, and its agentic story runs through A2UI: the GenUI SDK for Flutter "allows Flutter applications to connect to an Agent-to-Agent (A2UI) server and render dynamic user interfaces generated by an AI agent," composing widgets from a `Catalog` via `SurfaceController`, `A2uiTransportAdapter` and `BasicCatalogItems.asCatalog()` ([Flutter docs](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui/get-started)). Caveats: the docs still use older `genui` package names while packages ship as `a2ui_core`/`a2ui_flutter` ([SDKs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/)), and `PromptBuilder.chat()` can emit a 3,000–5,000+ token system prompt, a real constraint for on-device models.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — One action definition serves UI, agent, HTTP, MCP, A2A and CLI with shared validation and permissions, and `useActionQuery` infers types so no second implementation is needed ([docs](https://www.agent-native.com/docs/), [README](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native)); it solves agent sharing but is a TypeScript full-stack web framework, not a cross-platform UI toolkit.

**MUI** — A decade of battle-tested Material components with MUI X and an official `@mui/mcp` server ([README](https://github.com/mui/material-ui)); excellent for people, a documentation server for agents, nothing for native.

**Ouro UI** — The candidate that most literally answers the brief: "Ouro HX is how an app treats people, and Ouro AX is how it treats agents," with `ax-command`, `ax-claims`, `ax-xray` and a `ouro-check` that audits pages from 320 to 3840px in light and dark for overlap, clipped text, axe violations and motion jank ([Platforms](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/platforms/)); but HX is React/Tailwind copy-in so the human half is web-only, AX speaks CLI/HTTP/MCP rather than agent-authored visual UI, and "Ouro HX & AX for Android and for Windows are spare rooms with the lights on, waiting for a builder."

**Base UI** — Excellent unstyled primitives from the creators of Radix, Floating UI and Material UI, covered by the shared `@mui/mcp` server ([README](https://github.com/mui/base-ui)); superb for building a design system with full control, but web-only with no agent-renderable surface format.
actions.pullQuote: A2UI turns agent output into a design contract, then renders it natively on iOS, Android, Flutter and the web.
actions.testimonial: I chose A2UI because one artifact serves both audiences: a JSON Schema catalog that the agent SDK compiles into a model skill and each renderer implements natively, so a Material 3 catalog can drive Jetpack Compose while the same catalog drives SwiftUI and Flutter. The Catalog-Agnostic Accessibility Requirements, which oblige renderers to map the `@accessibility` envelope onto WAI-ARIA, Flutter Semantics and Android/iOS accessibility APIs, are what convince me the format serves people and agents at once rather than being agent-only markup. The honest trade-off is that A2UI is a protocol, not a beautiful component library: versus Ouro UI or shadcn/ui I still own the visual design, and a custom component today needs a hand-written implementation on each native platform. I accept that cost because the alternative is shipping native apps agents cannot shape.
